description: We are a team of three passionate problem solvers from Oman with a shared interest in technology, innovation, and space science. Our team combines skills in software development, artificial intelligence/machine learning, data analysis, research, UI/UX design, and creative problem solving. Through the NASA Space Apps Challenge, we aim to transform complex scientific data into an innovative, practical, and accessible solution with meaningful real-world impact.
summary:
Marswalk is a walk planner for the first crew on Mars. Astronauts leaving a base will cross ground nobody has walked on, with fixed power and oxygen, and Earth can’t help in real time. Every walk comes down to one question: can we get there and still get home?

We built Marswalk for a base at Three Forks in Jezero Crater, where Perseverance left its first sample depot. It combines four NASA datasets: HiRISE elevation (1 m), HiRISE imagery (25 cm), THEMIS night thermal from Mars Odyssey, and Perseverance’s traverse. Together they make a 10 m map of slope, roughness and ground type. A crew picks science stops, and Marswalk plans a fastest route and a conservative route. At every point of the route it checks that time, energy and oxygen, minus a reserve, still cover the walk home. When a stop is too steep, it says no, explains why, and offers a safe viewing point. Crews can also rehearse surprises by blocking a path and replanning.

We checked the map against Perseverance: 99.1% of the rover’s real track falls on ground we call walkable, and our route runs a median 22 m from its path. Next: live suit telemetry and Mars-suit data in place of Apollo’s.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?
Marswalk plans safe walks for the first crew on Mars, from a base at Three Forks in Jezero Crater, where Perseverance left its first sample depot. We combine four NASA datasets into a 10 m map of the area around the base:

  • HiRISE elevation (1 m) for slope and roughness;
  • HiRISE imagery (25 cm) for the base map and surface texture;
  • Mars Odyssey THEMIS night thermal to tell sand from rock, since rock stays warm after dark;
  • Perseverance’s traverse to check our results.

A random forest classifies each cell as sand, bedrock or rough. Steepness is always measured from elevation, never guessed from images. A crew picks science stops, and Marswalk plans two routes: a fastest one and a conservative one. At every point it checks that time, energy and oxygen, each minus a reserve, still cover the walk home. If a stop is too steep to stand on, it says so, explains why, and offers the nearest safe viewing point. A rehearsal mode lets crews block a path and replan.

What benefits does it have?

  • Crews and planners see before leaving whether a walk is safe, how long it takes, and how much margin remains.
  • When the answer is no, the planner says so plainly and gives the reason.
  • Rehearsal lets crews practise surprises on Earth before they happen on Mars.

What is the intended impact?
On Mars, a radio message to Earth takes minutes, so crews can’t rely on mission control in real time. Marswalk gives them their own tool for one of the most dangerous everyday tasks on Mars: walking outside and getting back. The pipeline works for any site with HiRISE elevation coverage, so it can help choose and plan future landing sites too.

What tools did we use?

  • Backend: Python with rasterio, NumPy, SciPy, scikit-image, scikit-learn, pandas, GeoPandas and Matplotlib, plus a lightweight Python web server.
  • Frontend: React, TypeScript, Vite and Leaflet.
  • Build and version control: a Makefile builds everything from the raw NASA files, and the code lives in Git and GitHub.
  • Hardware: our own laptops.
  • Data: all from NASA missions, through NASA and USGS Astrogeology.

How is it creative?
We used Perseverance as ground truth for planning human walks: 99.1% of the rover’s real track falls on ground our map calls walkable, and our route runs a median 22 m from its path. We use night-time thermal images to tell sand from rock. We also built a planner whose most important feature is refusing: one of our stops is steep on purpose, to show it won’t pretend unsafe ground is walkable.

What factors did our team consider?

  • Safety first: a reserve that is never spent, and the slope limit always comes from measured data.
  • NASA data only.
  • Honesty about limits: walking figures come from Apollo, a Moon stand-in; the classifier is modest at 67% against a 53% baseline; and the training labels were made with AI assistance and checked blind by our team.
  • Reproducibility: everything rebuilds from raw NASA data, offline, in about 30 seconds.
  • Clarity for the crew: every refusal comes with a reason.
